meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Show me a good loser and I'll show you a loser'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Vince Lombardi. No contemporary source ties it to him. The saying is anonymous, with good-loser talk in print by 1904 and a 1962 first exact match.

answer.label: Not Vince Lombardi — an anonymous coaching adage
answer.authorDates: A 20th-century sports adage · precursor recorded 1911, exact wording documented 1962
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator finds no contemporary citation linking this line to Vince Lombardi — the earliest attribution to him it located is a 2010 quotation compilation, four decades after his death. The saying evolved anonymously among American coaches and sportswriters, and the earliest exact match is credited to basketball player-coach Gus Doerner in April 1962.

source.excerpt: Show me a good loser and I’ll show you a loser.
trail: 1904–1911 — good-loser talk is already in print (an anonymous 1904 item, a 1907 column by “Jim Nasium”), and the earliest “show me a good loser” framing is recorded from Cincinnati Reds pitcher Harry Gaspar in May 1911, and in November 1924 Illinois coach Robert Zuppke publishes “a good loser is no good” in Liberty, the version Quote Investigator credits to him ↗.

1943 — Knute Rockne, dead twelve years, is credited with “Show me a good loser, and I will show you a failure” by his former publicity director George Strickler; more attributions follow in 1948 and 1957 ↗.
1962 — the exact modern wording appears, credited to basketball player-coach Gus Doerner; Red Auerbach receives credit for it in a 1965 UPI article, as documented by Quote Investigator ↗.
Today — Lombardi’s name is attached everywhere online, yet Wikiquote’s Lombardi page ↗ does not carry the line at all, and no speech, book, or interview has ever been cited for it.
source.excerptNote: There is no primary document to quote in context, because no source text has ever been produced for this line under Lombardi’s name. The wording above is the modern popular form, first matched exactly in 1962 — nearly fifty years before the earliest attribution to Lombardi that Quote Investigator could locate, a 2010 quotation compilation.

author.name: Vince Lombardi
author.heading: About Vince Lombardi
author.metaLine: 1913–1970 · NFL head coach, Green Bay Packers & Washington
author.bio: Vince Lombardi (June 11, 1913 – September 3, 1970) coached the Green Bay Packers from 1959 to 1967, winning five NFL championships in seven years and the first two Super Bowls, then spent a final season coaching in Washington before dying of cancer at 57. The Super Bowl trophy carries his name, and so — fairly or not — does a great deal of anonymous locker-room wisdom. He is one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced hard-nosed aphorisms, including this one and the more famous “Winning isn’t everything; it’s the only thing,” which researchers trace to coach Henry ‘Red’ Sanders in 1948.

misattribution.heading: Who it gets pinned on
misattribution.intro: This is a saying with many claimants and no owner. Three names dominate, and none of them holds up as the originator.

items.why: Quote-poster sites print it under his name with no speech, book, or interview attached. Quote Investigator found no contemporary citation ↗ — the earliest Lombardi attribution it located is a 2010 quotation compilation, forty years after his death.

Rockne died in 1931. The credit begins in 1943, when his former Notre Dame publicity director George Strickler reported him saying “Show me a good loser, and I will show you a failure” — not the modern wording — with further attributions following in 1948 and 1957 ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The creator is anonymous. The wording evolved for half a century, and the earliest exact match on record is Gus Doerner in April 1962, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: A coach’s creed that nobody actually wrote
lead: The idea is older than Lombardi’s whole career. In May 1911, Cincinnati Reds pitcher Harry Gaspar was quoted with a blunt precursor — a good loser, he said, was a darn fool — and in November 1924 University of Illinois football coach Robert Zuppke published the flat declaration that “a good loser is no good” in Liberty magazine, a line Quote Investigator credits to him ↗.

From there the thought kept mutating through decades of press boxes. In 1943 Knute Rockne’s former publicity director George Strickler put a version in the dead coach’s mouth — “show me a good loser, and I will show you a failure” — and the wording kept sliding until the modern form settled in the 1960s. That is what makes it a paraphrase without a parent: no single speaker invented it ↗.
context.detailsSummary: Why Lombardi ends up holding the bag
detailsBody: Lombardi is a gravitational attractor for competitive aphorisms. The best-known example is “Winning isn’t everything; it’s the only thing,” which Quote Investigator credits to Vanderbilt coach Henry ‘Red’ Sanders in November 1948 ↗; a December 1962 LIFE profile attached Sanders’s line to Lombardi, and it never came off. Lombardi’s own 1962 Esquire formulation was softer: wanting to win is what matters.

English Wikiquote’s Lombardi entry does not carry this good-loser line at all — not among its sourced quotations. The quote-poster sites that print it under his name supply no speech, book, or interview to check.
context.pull: The saying evolved for fifty years before anyone said it the way we quote it now.
